sources.title: Berthe Morisot (Q105320), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-20): English label 'Berthe Morisot', description 'French painter (1841-1895)', instance of human, born 14 January 1841, died 2 March 1895, citizen of France, Korean label 베르트 모리조. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

William MacKenzie, 'Morisot, Berthe (1841-1895)', Women in World History: A Biographical Encyclopedia (Gale; reproduced on Encyclopedia.com; read in full including its source list). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: calls her one of the most talented and prominent members of the Impressionist movement and follows her from the 1864 Salon through the Salon refusals of 1872 and 1873, the 1874 first group exhibition (the only woman among 30 artists), the 1875 auction, the 1883 Manet retrospective and the 1886 final exhibition to her 1892 solo show. Detailed reference biography drawing on the standard scholarship (Higonnet, Adler and Garb, Stuckey and Scott, her correspondence).

French Ministry of Culture, 'Les huit expositions impressionnistes 1874-1886: 1886, huitieme exposition' (collections-of-French-museums web page, read in full, in French). INDEPENDENT VOICE: reconstructs the preparation of the last Impressionist exhibition from letters by Pissarro and Guillaumin: with Caillebotte out and Degas hesitating, she alone had the means to finance it, applications were put to her, she visited the young Seurat and Signac and judged only the painting, and Pissarro wrote that without her and Degas there would be no exhibition.

Musee Marmottan Monet, 'Berthe Morisot' (permanent-collection page, read in full). Holder of the world's leading collection of her work by bequest of her descendants (25 oils, 75 watercolours, many pastels and drawings): calls her a student of Corot and muse of Manet, the first woman Impressionist and one of the main members of the group, notes she sold relatively few works, and credits her light colours, draughtsmanship and freedom of handling. Institutional praise; used only for scope and for the sales caveat.

Louise Sweeney, 'An Impressionist gets her due. A National Gallery show brings well-deserved luster to painter Berthe Morisot', The Christian Science Monitor, 21 September 1987 (read in full). Report on the first comprehensive US retrospective: curator Charles Stuckey calls her the boldest of the Impressionists and credits her with showing series of related works before Monet or Degas, Mount Holyoke's Teri Edelstein dissents and says she did not put herself forward and defined herself through her family, and the critic Paul Mantz is quoted calling her the only Impressionist in the group. Includes the 1896 memorial retrospective hung by Monet, Renoir and Degas and the reactions of Renoir and Pissarro to her death.

The Art Story, 'Berthe Morisot' (art-history encyclopedia entry with biography, read in full). Secondary compilation drawing on the standard biographies: Guichard's warning to her parents, the 1864 Salon, her influence on Manet's plein-air work, advice from Manet not to join the avant-garde, her exhibiting under her maiden name, Les XX in 1887, and the 1896 retrospective organised by her friends. It states some claims that other sources contradict (the year she missed, her sales, how alone she ran the 1886 show), so it is used only where others agree.

National Museum of Women in the Arts, 'Berthe Morisot' (artist profile, read). Museum profile: training with Corot and plein-air work, Salon submissions from 1864, the 1874 invitation to the first group show, the 1887 Georges Petit and New York exhibitions, and her turn to unprimed canvas around 1880 (with Manet and Eva Gonzales) that loosened her brushwork; notes that critics stressed 'feminine' qualities.

Biography.com Editors, 'Berthe Morisot Biography' (A&E Television Networks, updated 2019; read in full). General biography: her range of subjects and media (oil, watercolour, pastel, drawing), the 1874 decision to show with the Impressionists rather than at the Salon, her 1892 first solo exhibition and the 1894 purchase of 'Young Woman in a Ball Gown' by the French government, and her death from pneumonia on 2 March 1895. Popular and derivative; used for dates only.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_morisot_womenworld, src_morisot_culture | 1875-1886 | reference biography, ministry web page built on contemporaries' letters] The encyclopedia records that in 1875 she, Monet, Renoir and Sisley organised a public auction of their work, that in 1883 she and her husband organised a retrospective and sale of Manet's work after his death, and that in late 1885 she began preparing the last Impressionist exhibition and selected the artists to replace Renoir and Monet; the ministry page, from Pissarro's and Guillaumin's letters, shows her financing the 1886 show, vetting applicants and visiting Seurat and Signac. Two sources agree on 1886, but the earlier episodes rest on the encyclopedia alone, and a popular source's claim that she ran the 1886 show single-handed is contradicted by the ministry page. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 72 / 0.60 to 70 / 0.56 after the source-family check.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_morisot_womenworld, src_morisot_artstory, src_morisot_culture | 1874-1886 | reference biography, art-history encyclopedia, ministry web page] After the Salon jurors turned her down in 1872 and 1873 she joined the independent group show of 1874 at Degas's request, although Manet advised against it, and afterwards stopped sending to the Salon; in 1886 the ministry page, quoting Pissarro and Guillaumin, says she belonged to no clique, judged only the painting and was favourably disposed to the Divisionists' studies. The 1874 choice is told by sources from the same scholarly lineage; the 1886 impartiality is the ministry page's reading of letters from friends. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.56 to 66 / 0.52 because the 1874 decision is reported through one scholarly lineage and the 1886 impartiality is a reading of others' letters.

persistence.rationale: [src_morisot_womenworld, src_morisot_csm, src_morisot_biography | 1870-1895 | reference biography, press report on the 1987 retrospective, popular biography] During the 1870-71 siege, with troops quartered in her studio, she turned to watercolour and later left Paris to work on pictures that would sell; refused at the 1872 and 1873 Salons she kept exhibiting with the independent group and took part in all but one of the eight Impressionist exhibitions (the sources disagree on which year she missed, but place it around her daughter's birth); and a month after her husband's death in 1892 she held the solo exhibition he had encouraged. Several distinct episodes, but mostly from the encyclopedia.

collaboration.rationale: [src_morisot_womenworld, src_morisot_culture, src_morisot_csm | 1875-1896 | reference biography, ministry web page, press report] She organised the 1875 auction with Monet, Renoir and Sisley, worked with her husband on the Manet retrospective in 1883, and in 1886 arbitrated between the Degas and Pissarro groups (Pissarro's letters in the ministry page show the show hanging on her and Degas); her friends Monet, Renoir and Degas hung the 1896 memorial retrospective after her death (press report). Shared projects are documented, but how she worked with others day to day is not described, and the encyclopedia also records that she and Manet were not equals in the studio (he repainted her portrait of her mother and sister in 1870). SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.50 to 60 / 0.48 because shared-credit projects are reported mostly by one lineage and day-to-day collaboration is not described.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_morisot_csm, src_morisot_nmwa, src_morisot_artstory, src_morisot_marmottan | 1874-1891 | press report, museum profile, art-history encyclopedia, museum collection page] A contemporary critic called her the only Impressionist in the 1874 group and the curator Charles Stuckey calls her the boldest of the Impressionists and credits her with early series of related works (a claim from one curator that the other sources do not test); the women's museum notes her move to unprimed canvas around 1880, which loosened her brushwork, and the Marmottan praises her freedom of handling. Mostly retrospective assessment by admirers. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 70 / 0.56 to 66 / 0.50 because the 'boldest' and 'first series' claims are one curator's thesis and the rest is reputation, not a documented choice.

experimentation.rationale: [src_morisot_womenworld, src_morisot_nmwa, src_morisot_artstory, src_morisot_biography | 1871-1891 | reference biography, museum profile, art-history encyclopedia, popular biography] She worked in oil, watercolour, pastel and drawing (the encyclopedia says her watercolour and pastel work shaped her oil palette), tried unprimed canvas around 1880 and, in the early 1890s, painted a nude shepherdess outdoors, which a popular encyclopedia calls an unusual choice for a woman artist of the time; the encyclopedia also notes preparatory drawings after 1885, a more deliberate method than the group's supposed spontaneity. Several documented changes of method; sources are thin on how she tested ideas.

adaptability.rationale: [src_morisot_womenworld | 1870-1885 | reference biography] When troops were quartered in her studio in 1870-71 she switched to watercolour and pastel, which suited her; after the 1873 move she never kept a studio again and later worked in the living room of her own house, and in 1882 she left her exhibition submissions to her husband while she stayed at Nice. One source carries all of this, so it stays an inference.

achievement_drive.rationale: [src_morisot_womenworld, src_morisot_biography | 1871-1894 | reference biography, popular biography] The encyclopedia says that in 1871 she left Paris intent on painting pictures that would sell and links her drive to become a professional to the end of the civil war; she sold her first works to Durand-Ruel in 1872, exhibited at Brussels in 1887 and Petit's International Exhibition, and the French government bought a painting in 1894. Her professional ambition rests on one author's characterisation, and the Marmottan says she sold relatively few works. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 60 / 0.44 to 56 / 0.40 because the drive is one source's reading, not an instance documented by independent sources.

perfectionism.rationale: [src_morisot_artstory, src_morisot_womenworld | 1870-1890s | art-history encyclopedia, reference biography] The art-history encyclopedia calls her unrelentingly self-critical and quotes her letter to Monet saying she was at war with her canvases and doing nothing worthwhile; the reference biography records her frustration with the 1870 portrait of her mother and sister. Almost all of it is her own words or an editor's summary of them, so it is a weak signal. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 56 / 0.40 to 52 / 0.34 because the evidence is self-report.

portrait.source: Portrait of Berthe Morisot with a Fan, watercolour over traces of graphite on cream wove paper, Edouard Manet, 1874, 20.9 x 16.8 cm, Art Institute of Chicago, Helen Regenstein Collection, reference 1963.812 (record read on the museum's site and through its public API). The holder's own text names the sitter and says Manet represented his friend Berthe Morisot twelve times between 1868 and 1874. The file is the museum's 843-pixel-wide IIIF image (full size 4613 x 5588) with the white scan margin trimmed to 767 x 958: cropped only, not resized, not upscaled.

The lead's rights are clean (item record read: Public Domain, CC0; image-request page read: free for any purpose, credit 'Courtesy of the RISD Museum') but the usable image is a 900 x 1200 scan of a sheet with colour chart in which the 11.9 x 7.8 cm plate occupies only about 330 x 510 pixels, and higher resolution is by email request only; the museum site is now behind a Cloudflare challenge for plain requests (not bypassed; item and terms were read through the page reader, the scan through the public image link). Replacement: Manet's 1874 watercolour Portrait of Berthe Morisot with a Fan at the Art Institute of Chicago (1963.812), open-access CC0, 4613 x 5588 source; record and Terms read (CC0 images may be used for any purpose without further permission); the holder text names the sitter and the work is catalogued in the Manet catalogues raisonnes; the record lists no inscription, so the sitter rests on the holder's title and description, a likeness from life by a close friend and fellow painter. The artic.edu pages returned 403 to the page reader but were readable with a plain descriptive request (no bot wall or challenge). Dimensions: 843-wide IIIF derivative trimmed to 767 x 958; no upscaling. TERMS CHECKED: AIC Terms (https://www.artic.edu/terms) say images labelled CC0 may be used for any purpose without additional permission; the item is flagged is_public_domain in the AIC API; age basis independent (creator d.1883). Other leads checked and not used: Stage A Commons file 'Morisot berthe photo.jpg' (unknown author, date conflict), Manet's 1872 oil (Orsay, bot-walled), Desboutin drypoint c.1876 at AIC and the Met (not needed).
